Then resolve Q6's open amendments and think about architecture from the market research.

spec_round_protocol.why: Carried from the 2026-08-15/16 runs: one iteration authors the spec, the next reviews it cold, until a reviewer approves. The cap stops an artifact iterating forever.
spec_round_protocol.at_cap: APPROVE AND EXECUTE. This is a CHANGE from the previous run, made explicitly by the operator this session: 'one more change after the 3 round spec cap approve and execute.' Previously an artifact shipped at the cap with its objections recorded and was NOT implemented, which is why Q6 ended the last run at 0/21. Now, at the cap (or on earlier reviewer approval), record any outstanding objections in the change's own design.md AND proceed to implementation in the same run.

queue.title: Explore: what a specification corpus looks like at scale
queue.why: Operator, this session: improve the spec — 'think on how the spec will become once we start with a big project and we have different specs for different features. Maybe after finishing executing a delta as well to update all the specs, have a hierarchy on the specs.' Plus, on archive authority: 'be mindful of the folder trees and what not. The spec should still be useful. Also we need to be aware of the task board as well with time things will pile up there. Maybe make a task board by spec? I don't know.'
queue.detail: Write openspec/explorations/2026-08-16-a-corpus-at-scale.md. No code in this item. It must answer, with evidence from this repository rather than in the abstract: (1) What distinguishes a capability document from a change document, given the operator has ALREADY RULED that capability documents sit OUTSIDE the exploring/proposed/approved machine. (2) What the on-disk folder tree looks like once there are 30+ capabilities and hundreds of archived changes — openspec/specs/ has 30 capability specs today and openspec/changes/ has 17 unarchived changes, so both numbers are real and measurable now. The operator's test is 'the spec should still be useful', so navigability is the acceptance criterion, not tidiness. (3) What happens to the corpus when a delta finishes executing, given the operator has ALREADY RULED for an explicit authored merge over automatic requirement migration. (4) THE TASK BOARD AT SCALE. This is the operator's open question and the least-formed part of the brief. Ground it in the fact that Task.spec_document_id ALREADY EXISTS and is indexed (hub/hub/db/models.py:641), alongside Task.spec_task_key — so grouping or scoping the board by spec document is a query plus a UI affordance, NOT a schema change. Also ground it in taskFilterStore.activeTaskIds, which SpecCoverageBar already uses to filter the board from outside it (hub/ui/src/App.tsx:353). Recommend a shape and say what it costs. (5) What archiving should do to a change's tasks — they pile up on the board forever otherwise, which is precisely the operator's worry.
queue.output: One exploration document. It feeds N2 and N2b directly, so it must end in recommendations concrete enough to spec from, not a survey.

queue.title: KEYSTONE — spec then BUILD: the archive transition and the capability document kind
queue.why: This is the gap CLAUDE.md names as the reason openspec keeps the corpus: 'AgentWeave's lifecycle is exploring -> proposed -> approved with no archive phase and no concept of a current-behaviour specification. A document reaches approved and stops.' Closing it is what makes migrating off openspec possible at all. Everything else tonight is improvement; this changes what the product can be used for.
queue.detail: Full openspec change: proposal, design, tasks, spec delta — then IMPLEMENT it (see spec_round_protocol.at_cap). Ground facts, all verified this session, do not re-derive: hub/hub/spec_lifecycle.py defines exactly EXPLORING/PROPOSED/APPROVED (lines 28-30) and a four-entry TRANSITIONS set (34-42). SpecDocument.kind is already a free String(32) defaulting to 'change-spec' (models.py:1537) and NO second kind has ever been used — the slot exists and is vestigial. THE MIGRATION TRAP: SPEC_PHASES is enforced by a table-level CheckConstraint 'ck_spec_documents_phase' (models.py:1566-1569), and the comment immediately below it warns that a table-level CHECK naming a column makes that column UNDROPPABLE in SQLite. Adding a phase therefore needs a batch_alter_table recreate, in the shape of migrations 0035/0058/0073, NOT an ALTER. Migration head is 0073, so this is 0074, and it must guard for a missing table the way 0033/0034/0073 do. Bump the head assertions in BOTH hub/tests/test_migrations.py and hub/tests/test_project_persistence.py (CLAUDE.md). OPERATOR RULINGS, BINDING, DO NOT RE-LITIGATE: archiving is an OPERATOR act, mirroring the existing hard rule that an agent cannot approve — enforce it in spec_lifecycle.transition itself and not only at the API boundary, exactly as approval is enforced today, because 'a rule enforced in one place is a rule that survives exactly as long as nobody adds a second caller'. The corpus absorbs a finished change by EXPLICIT AUTHORED MERGE, not automatic requirement migration. Capability documents sit OUTSIDE the phase machine — kind='capability', no transitions, edited directly. Scope: migration + lifecycle + API + UI. Must not weaken the existing approval rule. OPERATOR RULING ON THE ONE OPEN SCHEMA QUESTION, taken this session: a capability document carries a DEDICATED phase value with NO outgoing or incoming transitions — a fourth value (e.g. 'current') that the TRANSITIONS table never names. Rejected: parking capability documents at 'approved' forever with the UI hiding the phase bar, because the row would then lie about what it is, and a reader of the database could not tell a capability document from a change that happens to be approved. `phase` is NOT NULL under a CHECK constraint, so some value is unavoidable; this makes it an honest one. Migration 0074 therefore adds TWO values to ck_spec_documents_phase: 'archived' and the capability phase.
queue.output: A merged openspec change with its tasks implemented, both suites green, openspec validate --changes --strict clean.

queue.title: Spec then BUILD: many named loops as a first-class Hub concept — model, API, visibility (composing AgentWeave's own primitives)
queue.why: Operator, this session: 'Improving the job system with more visibility, traceability and the ability to do better then what we're doing now with the loop that we do.' The loop that runs this very session is not in the product.
queue.detail: Ground facts, verified this session: AIJob (models.py:1123) is project + agent + ONE message string + cron + session_mode('new'|'resume') + enabled. JobRun (models.py:1160) records only fired_at, status ('fired'|'failed'), trigger ('scheduled'|'manual'), session_id, error_summary. That is the whole job system. Everything that makes the overnight loop actually work lives in .claude/autonomous/STATE.json on disk, outside the product: an ordered queue with per-item status and why/detail, a current item, next_action written for a stranger, limits, decisions_for_user, iteration count, heartbeat, stop_at, stop_when_queue_empties, and a narrative log. Model the new concepts on THAT proven shape — it is a working design validated over three overnight runs, not a guess. PRE-AUTHORISED DEFAULT: add new tables rather than overloading AIJob/JobRun, and leave the existing scheduler path working unchanged; cost if wrong is a later consolidation migration, which is cheaper than breaking scheduled jobs at 3am. SCOPE CEILING, set by the operator: model + API + visibility ONLY. The Hub actually spawning or re-entering iterations is EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE — the run must not build the thing that would drive it, and could not test that unattended anyway. Include a UI that makes a run legible: what fired, what each iteration did, what it produced, what it decided, why it stopped. ===== TWO OPERATOR NOTES ADDED AT APPROVAL, both binding and both changing the shape of this item. NOTE 1 — 'take inspiration on what we use today but take advantage of agentweave.' STATE.json is the proven SHAPE, not the design to port wholesale. The Hub already models most of what STATE.json reinvents on disk, and the job system should COMPOSE with those primitives rather than build a parallel universe beside them. Map it deliberately, and justify any place you decide NOT to reuse: STATE.json's `decisions_for_user` is the Hub's existing questions table and QuestionsPanel (hub/hub/api/v1/questions.py, ask_user); an iteration is already a Run, with a conversation, output logs, turn_usage and cost accounting attached; a queue item is close to a Task, which already has status, assignee, transitions and spec_document_id; the loop's narrative log is close to agent_outputs plus the activity timeline; a loop's operator is an Agent bound to a Runner and a Charter, which is how every other execution in this product is addressed. A job system that re-implements questions, runs and tasks under new names would be the single biggest architectural mistake available tonight. NOTE 2 — 'remember that we can have loops for multiple things. Shorter dev loops that keeps developing and longer loops that will do security scans, etc.' The model is therefore MANY NAMED LOOPS, not one global run. Several may exist and be enabled at once, each with its own cadence, its own purpose, its own queue and its own scope — a tight development loop iterating every few minutes alongside a nightly security scan alongside a weekly dependency audit. AIJob already carries a per-job `cron`, so differing cadence is already expressible at the job level; what is missing is the loop semantics layered on top, and the fact that those semantics must be PER-LOOP rather than global. Nothing in the design may assume a singleton: not the queue, not the iteration counter, not the stop condition, not the UI. The visibility surface must let the operator see several loops at once and tell at a glance which is advancing, which is waiting on them, and which has stopped.
queue.output: A spec'd and implemented change. Existing scheduled jobs must still work — prove it with the existing tests, not by assertion.
